The takeaway is that culture, word-of-mouth recruitment, and even philanthropic spending can drive growth and brand strength more effectively than conventional advertising, tying hiring to the broader mission and customer service ethos.
video-request-ks70k37hb3twzyk61cmpdx0zjs.title: Jeanne Bliss - Do You Hire People Who Fit the Soul of Your Company?

video-request-ks70k37hb3twzyk61cmpdx0zjs.summary: Jeanne Bliss frames apologies as a disciplined practice: taking accountability, repairing the connection with humility and remorse, and embedding those behaviors into an organization's culture. She then outlines a practical three-part framework to decide when to say sorry: first, establish a cross-functional, daily overview-style process so all teams have visibility during customer audits or incidents; second, actively solicit what frontline staff need when handling customer calls; and third, implement a proactive customer recovery plan analogous to an IT recovery plan to guide timely, transparent remediation.
video-request-ks70k37hb3twzyk61cmpdx0zjs.title: Jeanne Bliss -Three Actions to Earn Back Customer Trust

video-request-ks70k37hb3twzyk61cmpdx0zjs.summary: In this short interview, Jeanne Bliss articulates a practical framework for building “beloved” companies. She identifies three differentiators: (1) customers who tell your story in the marketplace, which creates competitive immunity; (2) employees who stay, which lowers recruiting costs and sustains Energy; and (3) an unrivaled customer experience that fuels profitability and growth in both good and bad times. She emphasizes that customer love and social proof—exemplified by positive mentions in social media—are key signals, and she cautions that CRM alone is not a magic bullet. To be effective, organizations must blend high-touch engagement with high-tech data and ensure action and accountability flow from insights, not just collection of information.
video-request-ks70k37hb3twzyk61cmpdx0zjs.title: Jeanne Bliss Interview

video-request-ks70k37hb3twzyk61cmpdx0zjs.summary: Jeanne Bliss introduces a five-step decision assessment that asks viewers to benchmark their company decisions against five decisions made by beloved brands. The aim is to reveal how externally perceived decisions influence loyalty, growth, and overall brand image, and to show how such decisions can be oriented toward both customers and employees. The talk emphasizes that at each decision point (the “fork in the road”) observers will see how beloved companies guide their choices and how those decisions are operationally executed within the organization to drive devoted customers and sustainable growth.
video-request-ks70k37hb3twzyk61cmpdx0zjs.title: Jeanne Bliss - Introduction to 5 Decision Assessment

video-request-ks70k37hb3twzyk61cmpdx0zjs.summary: In this talk, Jeanne Bliss argues that genuine customer focus starts with reliable operations and grows through emotional connections and frontline empowerment. She cites Land’s End as an example of operational reliability—quick phone responses and 24-hour shipping—as a foundation for differentiated customer experiences. She describes a playful packaging gesture for land’s End Kids that reinforces family values, then shifts to a broader framework of customer-centric leadership: treat customers as living, breathing people, start product decisions from emotion, and use a “customer math” approach that answers five questions about customers (including newest and lost customers) to keep the organization aligned around customers. The talk culminates in a contrast with Zappos, where frontline staff are trusted as heroes, including a generous 365-day return policy that fuels word-of-mouth growth. Together, these examples illustrate how reliability, emotional branding, and frontline autonomy translate into loyalty and long-term growth.
video-request-ks70k37hb3twzyk61cmpdx0zjs.title: Jeanne Bliss: Passion

video-request-ks70k37hb3twzyk61cmpdx0zjs.summary: In this 38-second talk published May 8, 2013, Jeanne Bliss argues that social media success hinges on operational reliability. She states that reliability across the front line, processes, and response times creates a trust-worthy customer experience, because your reliability is what gives customers a story to tell: "in social media, your ability to be reliable is what gives your customers a story to tell." The talk highlights specific reliability touchpoints—quality of staff, process reliability, how long it takes to answer a phone, and cycle time to deliver the first review—and invites organizations to assess their current reliability to turn service consistency into a compelling social narrative.
video-request-ks70k37hb3twzyk61cmpdx0zjs.title: Jeanne Bliss - Experience Reliability Gives You a Story to Tell in Social Media

video-request-ks70k37hb3twzyk61cmpdx0zjs.summary: The speaker argues that teams should not rush to begin projects; the first priority is to unite the leadership team because leaders often measure success using their own metrics. The recommended approach is to bring the leadership together to assess the reliability of each stage of the customer experience from a single, company-wide perspective, acknowledging that the current “one company experience” is not reliably delivered yet. The ultimate aim is to improve the customer’s life so they will share the experience with others and seek it again, thereby driving advocacy and repeat engagement.
video-request-ks70k37hb3twzyk61cmpdx0zjs.title: Jeanne Bliss On "Uniting the C Suite"

video-request-ks70k37hb3twzyk61cmpdx0zjs.summary: Jeanne Bliss presents a practical framework for turning customer-centric rhetoric into a repeatable, revenue-driving growth engine. She argues that most organizations are siloed and deliver inconsistent experiences unless work is broken into bite-sized, cross-functional efforts focused on reliable performance in the moments that matter. The talk traces roots of the discipline (moments of truth) through SAS Airlines, Lands’ End, and other case studies, then introduces five competencies for leading a customer-centric organization: treating customers as assets, defining journey stages, building a disciplined listening path, preempting unreliability, and ensuring leadership accountability. She peppered the talk with concrete tactics (touchpoint mapping, ‘kill a stupid rule,’ the customer room, storytelling by stage, and Vulcan mind meld exercises) and illustrated how reliability precedes delight, how to converge customer data into actionable insights, and how to structure governance to sustain a culture of customer growth.
video-request-ks70k37hb3twzyk61cmpdx0zjs.title: Jeanne Bliss Keynote: "Building Your Customer-Driven Growth Engine"

video-request-ks70k37hb3twzyk61cmpdx0zjs.summary: Jeanne Bliss describes how a company becomes 'beloved' by uniting actions and goals across organizational silos to improve the customer experience. The talk emphasizes that customer impact is enhanced when cross-functional teams share ownership of the customer experience, adopt common and sometimes uncomfortable metrics, and replace siloed ownership with collaborative, process-driven rigor. A billing example illustrates how multiple departments influence a single touchpoint, while Bliss ties the approach to her Chief Customer Officer framework and advocates breaking change into bite-sized steps to make durable progress.
video-request-ks70k37hb3twzyk61cmpdx0zjs.title: Beloved companies unite actions & goals

video-request-ks70k37hb3twzyk61cmpdx0zjs.summary: This succinct clip presents a leadership-focused reflection on authenticity. Jeanne Bliss asks whether leaders connect with people in a human way and whether they foster an environment that lets employees bring their best selves to work. The introspective questions frame authenticity as foundational to a workplace culture that can feel like a business home, where decisions align with personal values and life outside the office.
video-request-ks70k37hb3twzyk61cmpdx0zjs.title: Jeanne Bliss - How Real Are You?

video-request-ks70k37hb3twzyk61cmpdx0zjs.summary: This six-minute introduction showcases Jeanne Bliss outlining her credentials and core philosophy for leading customer experience in large organizations. The talk foregrounds the idea that customer loyalty is driven by a desirable experience rather than mere satisfaction, introduces the iconic “stairway to desire,” and emphasizes cross-functional alignment to break silos. It weaves in real-world references (Rackspace example, public publications, and Bliss’s book) and culminates with actionable guidance for speakers and organizations to drive accountability for the customer experience, including an exercise to simulate unified leadership in a conference setting.
video-request-ks70k37hb3twzyk61cmpdx0zjs.title: Jeanne Bliss: Introduction

video-request-ks70k37hb3twzyk61cmpdx0zjs.summary: The video presents a Southwest Airlines example of proactive customer experience recovery. Each day the airline reviews the prior day’s flights to identify whether a passenger’s life was interrupted, regardless of fault. A cross‑functional team—including operations staff, meteorologists, and a labeled “chief forgiveness officer”—assesses disruption severity and may respond with a preemptive apology letter and, in some cases, a monetary gesture called a love buck to encourage future travel. The speaker contrasts this approach with conventional “finance-only” thinking, noting Southwest still achieved a net revenue increase of about $1.7 million from these goodwill gestures, illustrating how proactive recovery can align customer satisfaction with financial outcomes.
video-request-ks70k37hb3twzyk61cmpdx0zjs.title: Jeanne Bliss - How Proactive Are You in Customer Experience Recovery?

video-request-ks70k37hb3twzyk61cmpdx0zjs.summary: Jeanne Bliss argues that modern organizations have become siloed, with marketing, operations, and sales excelling in their disciplines while customers move across the entire journey. She proposes placing a central function to orchestrate a holistic, one-company customer experience. The video highlights social media as a powerful revealer of the total customer experience, beyond traditional service metrics. Bliss teaches that insights should be drawn from the lives of customers and validated with numeric survey data, but the story should be led by the lived experience rather than by the score alone.
video-request-ks70k37hb3twzyk61cmpdx0zjs.title: Jeanne Bliss On "Using Social Media"

video-request-ks70k37hb3twzyk61cmpdx0zjs.summary: The speaker discusses Colleen Barrett’s role at Southwest Airlines and frames leadership around being real and human, grounded in servant leadership. The narrative juxtaposes Southwest’s rising customer satisfaction with a rival claim from Northwest Airlines and describes an official corporate response, followed by a lighthearted tone that emphasizes humor and whimsy as a deliberate daily practice. Together, these elements illustrate how culture, communication, and leadership style contribute to Southwest’s authenticity and customer focus.
video-request-ks70k37hb3twzyk61cmpdx0zjs.title: Jeanne Bliss - How Southwest Airlines Decided to Be Real

Through concrete examples (Zane Cycles’ test ride policy; a shoe merchant’s community impact; Edward Jones’ advisor handoff), the talk links these behaviors to lasting customer relationships, culture, and measurable lifetime value. It contrasts product-centric thinking with experiential, human-centered design, and ends with a call to action: decide who you are and what you value in customer interactions.

video-request-ks70k37hb3twzyk61cmpdx0zjs.summary: In a concise 98-second talk, Jeanne Bliss outlines three actions to embed clarity of purpose into a business. She advocates starting with bookend customer experiences to engage mid-level staff in shaping the most meaningful entry and exit moments, challenging legacy practices, and pushing for a more personal connection with customers. She then emphasizes hiring for memory-making ability—looking for candidates who can create memorable moments and demonstrate it in storytelling or a concrete example. Finally, she pitches the role of a cruise director or navigator who guides customers through organizational complexity, with the guidance turning into memory that delivers peace of mind and, in turn, drives business growth.

video-request-ks70k37hb3twzyk61cmpdx0zjs.summary: Jeanne Bliss outlines five core decisions that distinguish beloved companies in their relationships with customers and employees: believe, with suspending cynicism; decide with clarity of purpose and align actions to a higher service-oriented promise; be real by shedding corporate veneer and creating an environment where employees can bring their best selves; be there by showing up for customers every day in ways that earn their loyalty; and repair the emotional connection after mistakes, moving beyond perfunctory apologies. Bliss links these practices to both financial prosperity and the prosperity of the human spirit, noting that genuine care generates customer loyalty and a energetic, magnet-like workplace culture. The talk contrasts sincere, repair-focused apologies with hollow ones and cites two years of research supporting the link between deliberate people-first decisions and better outcomes.
video-request-ks70k37hb3twzyk61cmpdx0zjs.title: Jeanne Bliss: 5 Decisions Beloved Companies Make

video-request-ks70k37hb3twzyk61cmpdx0zjs.summary: Jeanne Bliss presents three concrete actions to hardwire belief in an organization's core competency: first, revamp hiring by starting with core values and adopting values-based screening (citing Chick-fil-A as an example); second, launch a “kill-a-stupid rule” movement to expose and eliminate outdated legacy rules, rewarding transparency and even celebrating successful removals with employee engagement; and third, share financials with all employees to build trust, with Container Store cited as an example of open financial reporting within a private company.
video-request-ks70k37hb3twzyk61cmpdx0zjs.title: Jeanne Bliss - Three Actions that Help Build a Culture of "Belief" in Your Organization

video-request-ks70k37hb3twzyk61cmpdx0zjs.summary: In this excerpt from Jeanne Bliss’s talk, Zara is presented as a concrete example of how beloved, prosperous companies sustain magnetic momentum through deliberate business actions. The speaker notes that top brands prune their product lines aggressively (even cutting a hundred products annually) to focus on what customers truly love, while still creating a compelling offer. Zara is highlighted for its ability to break even in a new store within about three months, and for driving high customer touchpoints—visits averaging 17 per year—through a deliberate store and product experience. The overall message emphasizes knowing customers’ lives to serve them effectively, maintaining a continuous, lifecycle-aware product and service experience, and engaging with customers personally in business relationships.
video-request-ks70k37hb3twzyk61cmpdx0zjs.title: Jeanne Bliss: Characteristics of 3 Beloved and Prosperous Companies

video-request-ks70k37hb3twzyk61cmpdx0zjs.summary: In this brief interview excerpt, Alfred Lin discusses Zappos’ strategic shift from a dropshipping model to stocking inventory in order to better control the customer experience. The team explains how the original plan—market on the web and pass orders to brand partners for shipment—carried the appeal of no inventory costs, but many brand manufacturers blocked that approach. As a result, Zappos began inventorying more products and found that owning fulfillment enabled a noticeably better customer experience. The pivotal decision to stop dropshipping required sacrificing about 25% of revenue and increasing capital and cash needs, a trade-off deemed worthwhile for service and growth. Governance around the pivot was relatively uncomplicated by comparison, since there were few outside investors and the founders were effectively the board at the time. The tour moment also showcases a confession bell used to engage participants, adding a light aside to the otherwise strategic discussion.

video-request-ks70k37hb3twzyk61cmpdx0zjs.summary: In this interview excerpt, Alfred Lin of Zappos discusses the company's enduring focus on exceptional customer service as a growth engine. The conversation covers enabling front-line reps to locate out-of-stock shoes across multiple sites (a proactive, customer-first approach), the company’s core value of delivering 'wow through service,' and the belief that long-term customer relationships trump individual sales. The dialogue also frames the cost of great service in branding terms, noting an average call length of five to six minutes and arguing that the branding value of a positive customer experience outweighs the incremental costs. The exchange references the Miracle on 34th Street analogy to illustrate proactive service and cites downturn-era resilience in 2008–2009 as part of Zappos’ sustained growth.
video-request-ks70k37hb3twzyk61cmpdx0zjs.title: Jeanne Bliss interviews Alfred Lin of Zappos

video-request-ks70k37hb3twzyk61cmpdx0zjs.summary: Jeanne Bliss presents a concise leadership approach that centers frontline empowerment: give frontline staff the authority to act from their heart and gut to make guiding decisions for customers. The talk emphasizes starting with belief in people, aligning actions with a clear higher purpose for customers, and maintaining real, human interactions while being operationally deliberate to identify where service breakdowns occur. The speaker argues that apologies should be the last resort, used to repair the emotional connection once the underlying issues are understood. The message is supported by a brief business example referencing L.L. Bean's performance, illustrating how customer-centric frontline behavior can correlate with strong company results, such as substantial annual sales (about 1.5 billion).
video-request-ks70k37hb3twzyk61cmpdx0zjs.title: Jeanne Bliss - Can Your Frontline Rescue Customers?

video-request-ks70k37hb3twzyk61cmpdx0zjs.summary: This short, lecture‑style message argues that sustained prosperity comes from being consistently present for customers and adopting their point of view. By prioritizing reliability and designing experiences around what matters to customers, brands earn the right to grow and become beloved. The speaker anchors the idea with a nod to Amazon’s early reliability (doing books right in 1995) and then exhorts leaders to imagine customers’ lives, understand what matters to them, and act accordingly to deliver peace of mind. The conclusion asks viewers to assess their own current standing relative to these principles and prompts customer advocacy through memorable experiences that customers will tell others about.
video-request-ks70k37hb3twzyk61cmpdx0zjs.title: Jeanne Bliss -  Decide To Be There (Decision 4)

video-request-ks70k37hb3twzyk61cmpdx0zjs.summary: In this interview excerpt, Ray Davis describes the strategic shift in 1990s to a store-centric, customer-friendly banking model designed to differentiate from large, product-focused banks. He explains how the “store” concept reframed product delivery, hiring, and culture around empowering front-line staff, creativity within rules, and a transparent, accountability-driven leadership style. The discussion covers recruitment in retail rather than banking, the evolving culture as the organization’s greatest asset and its greatest risk, and how clear communication—down to salary decisions—maintains alignment during growth and during acquisitions. Across the narrative, the emphasis is on experiential banking, cross-industry learning, and staying dynamic rather than becoming a bureaucracy-driven traditional bank.

The new attitude—treating passengers as honored guests—permeates the organization and is linked to a dramatic competitive outcome in the Canadian market within five years. video-request-ks70k37hb3twzyk61cmpdx0zjs.summary: In this short talk, Jeanne Bliss outlines a five-competency framework intended to transform customer experience work from a reactive, survey-driven activity into a growth engine for the business. Additional competencies cover building a comprehensive customer listening path from multiple feedback sources, instituting proactive and repeatable experience reliability with a rigorous CX design method, and ensuring leadership decisions, hiring, and policy environments align with deliberate growth. Together, these elements are presented as an organizational engine to drive sustained growth through improved customer experience.
